g.text: C219 · Figure 1.9 — three ways to put a laser on a silicon chip

text.style: font-size: 8.8px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #a1a1a6

g.text: Silicon chips lack an on-chip light source, so laser light has to be added: bond the gain on, shine it in, or co-package it (§1.4.4, book p.15)

g.text: waveguide; the mode's evanescent tail leaks into the Si.

g.text: Also in the text, not drawn: III-V grown epitaxially on Si, and germanium as a CMOS-compatible gain medium, where strain + heavy n-type doping

g.text: overcome the small (134 meV) difference between its indirect and direct band gaps — more in Chapter 8.

text.style: font-weight: 700; font-size: 9px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #f6f6f6

g.text: Takeaway: all products on the market today use simpler routes, e.g. (b) a fibre-connected off-chip laser or (c) a laser co-packaged with the chip.

text.style: font-size: 8.9px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #f6f6f6

g.text: (a) puts gain on the chip, but III-V materials clash with the standard CMOS process, bonding is costly and low-yield, and III-V wafers are small.
